Definition: An ADR is a record of a decision as it stood at the moment it was made; if the decision is later reversed, that is a new decision with its own record, not an edit to the old one.
When to use: Use where the participant frames an ADR's identity around the moment of decision ('point in time', 'chronological record') as opposed to a living or evolving document.
When not to use: Use Immutability and superseding instead when the point is specifically the never-rewrite rule or the supersession mechanism, not the definitional framing itself.

Code: Context and rationale for the decision
Definition: A good ADR lets a reader recover both the situation the decision responded to and the reasoning that led from it to the choice made. The situation and the reasoning are coded together, because in practice the participants do not separate them.
When to use: Use for statements about what context/rationale should contain, how large a share of the ADR it should be, or why the reader needs it to judge or re-examine the decision later.
When not to use: Use Missing rationale instead when the point is that this content is absent from a specific ADR. Use Explicit trade-off acceptance when the content is specifically a named, accepted sacrifice rather than the general reasoning.

Definition: ADRs are written so that people later in time (including the authors' future selves) can recover why a decision was made. Distinct from Future-reader benefit observed: this code is the stated purpose, not a report of the purpose actually being fulfilled.
When to use: Use for abstract statements of intent: 'we write them so that...', 'so that people later on can examine...'
When not to use: Use Future-reader benefit observed instead for concrete, reported instances of a later reader actually being helped.

Definition: The act of writing the record improves the decision itself, by forcing articulation of alternatives and trade-offs the author might otherwise leave implicit.
When to use: Use where the benefit named accrues to the author at the time of writing, not to a later reader.
When not to use: Use Rationale for future readers instead when the benefit is for a later reader.

Definition: A high-quality ADR clearly identifies the design issue or question that required a decision, as its own element distinct from the alternatives weighed or the decision taken.
When to use: Use where the participant names the issue/problem as a structural element in its own right: 'first, what is the issue', 'the design issue... is essentially the structure'.
When not to use: Use Context and rationale for the decision instead for the surrounding situation and reasoning, once the issue itself is not the point being made. Do not force this code onto participants who describe the structure of a record without an explicit issue field; that absence is itself worth preserving.

Definition: The options weighed before the decision are recorded as part of the ADR.
When to use: Use for the presence of alternatives as content, including a reader's expectation that alternatives be discussed.
When not to use: Use Rejected alternatives and why instead when the emphasis is specifically on preserving why the discarded options were discarded: the participant who discusses this at length treats it as a harder, more valuable thing than merely listing options, so the two are kept apart rather than merged.

Definition: Not merely listing options not taken, but preserving the argument for rejecting them: named explicitly as difficult to do and unusually valuable when done.
When to use: Use where the participant asks for, or singles out, the reasoning behind rejection as distinct from the list of alternatives itself.
When not to use: Use Alternatives considered instead for a bare list with no emphasis on the rejection reasoning.

Definition: The record states, as an act of transparency, what is knowingly being given up: a quality accepted as weaker in exchange for something else.
When to use: Use where the participant frames this as a conscious, named acceptance of a sacrifice ('we explicitly accept that X may not be good'), not merely a listing of effects.
When not to use: Use Consequences as factual outcomes instead for the general prescription that consequences be declarative; this code is specifically the named, accepted trade-off.

Definition: What will be different as a result of the decision, stated declaratively rather than evaluatively: a statement of fact, not a pro or a con.
When to use: Use for statements about what the consequences section should contain or how it should read, including bare mentions of writing down implications.
When not to use: Use Consequences reduced to pros and cons instead when the point is the failure mode: consequences written as evaluations.

Code: Grounding in critical use cases and quality attributes
Definition: Decisions are tied to the small number of use cases, quality attributes, or non-functional requirements that define what the system must do, so a reader can see what the decision serves.
When to use: Use where usefulness or reasoning is made conditional on this binding, including 'the top three/five use cases' formulations and general NFR-driven framing of the whole approach.
When not to use: Use Context and rationale for the decision instead for context that is not specifically tied to named use cases or quality attributes.

Definition: The record carries, or points at, the concrete implementation artefact the decision produced, so the claim can be checked against what was actually built.
When to use: Use for including data structures, diagrams, or traces alongside the decision, and for the claim that what an ADR asserts should be visible in the implementation.
When not to use: Use Boundary with supporting documents instead when the question is where full design detail should live (linked out vs inline), rather than whether the implementation itself should be traceable to the decision.

Definition: The ADR carries its own approval state (accepted, superseded, amended) as a document-level field, distinct from the never-rewrite rule that governs it.
When to use: Use for the status field itself and for status pointing at a superseding or amending decision.
When not to use: Use Immutability and superseding instead for the rule that content is not rewritten. Use Desired tool capability instead for per-element completeness tracking within a single still-open ADR (open implications, unresolved issues), which is a different thing from the ADR's own accepted or superseded state.

Definition: A template or fixed set of sections (issue, alternatives, decision, consequences, context, status) helps the writer think and the reader navigate.
When to use: Use where structure is described as useful, or where the participant enumerates the sections or fields they use.
When not to use: Use Structure dispensable for the experienced instead where the point is that structure is optional or inferior for some writers or audiences.

Definition: Experienced writers can carry the same content in free-flowing prose; explicit sectioning is a crutch for the less experienced, sometimes even a worse read.
When to use: Use where explicit structure is called optional, hidden, or unnecessary for some writers or contexts.
When not to use: Use Structure as scaffolding instead when structure is endorsed rather than made optional.

Definition: The ADR as a whole should be short and readable quickly; even a one-line rationale can be sufficient if it explains the why.
When to use: Use for length or simplicity prescriptions about the document as a whole ('read it in a few minutes', 'keep it simple'), including the claim that a minimal explanation suffices.
When not to use: Use Assertive active voice instead for the grammatical register of the decision statement specifically, and Decision section as design document for the anti-pattern of the decision section growing too large. Conciseness and voice are kept apart even where they occur in the same utterance, because they are different properties.

Definition: The decision statement is phrased actively and authoritatively ('we will do X') because passive constructions hide who acts and who is affected.
When to use: Use for grammatical prescriptions specifically about voice and agency in the decision statement.
When not to use: Use Brevity and simplicity instead for length or overall-document simplicity claims.

Definition: The register is expository, not advocacy: the ADR describes a decision, it does not sell it, pitch it, or make an emotional appeal.
When to use: Use for statements against persuasive writing, pitch-deck framing, or emotional appeal in ADR text.
When not to use: Use Consequences reduced to pros and cons instead when the failure is specifically that consequences (not the decision statement) are phrased evaluatively.

Definition: Where full design detail lives relative to the ADR: linked out to keep the ADR light, or deliberately embedded so the ADR is self-contained. The two participants take opposite positions on this; it is kept as one code because it is the same question, not two.
When to use: Use for the editorial choice of linking versus embedding supporting design material.
When not to use: Use Storage discoverability and canonical location instead for where the canonical *record itself* lives and how it is found: a repository/platform question, not a content-boundary one.

Definition: ADR quality is a special case of general technical writing and communication skill, which the participant sees as under-taught or in decline.
When to use: Use where writing ability itself, rather than any specific element or rule, is named as the determinant of ADR quality.
When not to use: Use the specific Form codes instead for individual, nameable style rules.

Definition: The record states a decision whose reasoning the reader cannot reconstruct, leaving an obvious 'why not the other option?' unanswered.
When to use: Use where the absence of the why is described as the defect, including worked examples.
When not to use: Use Context and rationale for the decision instead for the positive requirement.

Definition: The decision section is inflated into a full design document or decision matrix, defeating the format's purpose.
When to use: Use where over-long or over-detailed decision content is named as a misuse of the format.
When not to use: Use Brevity and simplicity instead for a general preference for short records with no specific misuse named.

Definition: Content that does not belong in an ADR for a different reason than length: speculation in the RFC sense, or material serving an inter-team political argument. Kept apart from Decision section as design document: the participant who names both treats them as two distinct exclusions ('the other thing that should not go in the ADR is...'), not two symptoms of one problem.
When to use: Use for explicit exclusion of speculative or political content.
When not to use: Use Decision section as design document instead when the excluded material is design detail rather than speculation or politics.

Code: Consequences reduced to pros and cons
Definition: Consequences written as evaluations rather than facts, importing the writer's subjective stance into what should be a declarative record.
When to use: Use where pro/con framing is identified as the specific error.
When not to use: Use Consequences as factual outcomes instead for the positive prescription.

Definition: Records are written and then never returned to; documentation decays or goes missing, observed as a problem rather than proposed as something to fix.
When to use: Use for observations of decay, abandonment, or outdated documentation.
When not to use: Use Periodic review of the log instead once the participant is describing the remedy (a practice of revisiting) rather than the problem. The two may co-occur in the same turn where a participant pivots from problem to proposal; that is a legitimate dual-code, not an error.

Definition: An ADR written after the decision has already taken effect tends toward a flattering, reconstructed account: consequences are known rather than anticipated, context is misremembered, and past selves are credited with wisdom they may not have had.
When to use: Use for memory distortion, rosy hindsight, self-presentation bias, or the effort required to stay intellectually honest about what was known at the time, in a retrospectively written ADR.
When not to use: Use Generated rationale is not the real rationale instead when the distorted account comes from a model rather than a person reconstructing their own past decision.

Definition: Decisions are not taken at a planned moment; they emerge from lower-level discussion and are recognised as decisions, and as occasions to write something down, only once under way or already made.
When to use: Use for descriptions of ADRs or decisions arising from POC work, lower-level discussion, or recognition after the fact rather than from a fixed decision queue.
When not to use: Use Retrospective ADR bias instead once the participant is specifically describing the distortions that late writing introduces, rather than the timing mechanism itself.

Definition: The record passes through stages (collaborative drafting, then acceptance, then publication to a canonical location) with the artefacts used at each stage.
When to use: Use for descriptions of the stages a record moves through and what happens at each.
When not to use: Use Wiki and document tooling instead for the tools themselves considered independently of the workflow stages, and Storage discoverability and canonical location for the question of where the canonical version lives once published.

Definition: An accepted ADR is not rewritten; a reversal or amendment is a new, linked decision, and the mechanism for tracking that is the status field pointing at the superseding record.
When to use: Use for the never-rewrite rule and for supersession/amendment as the mechanism of change.
When not to use: Use Status and lifecycle marking instead for the status field considered as a document element in itself, and Periodic review of the log for the practice of checking whether a supersession is now warranted.

Definition: When and why people actually open existing ADRs (joining a team, a reorganisation, facing a related decision, a downstream team asking why), described as observed behaviour.
When to use: Use for descriptions of when/why ADRs get read, including how rarely this happens.
When not to use: Use Future-reader benefit observed instead when the point is that the consultation was helpful, not merely that it happened. The two commonly co-occur in the same turn and may be double-coded.

Definition: Organisational machinery around ADRs: who owns templates and guidance, formal architecture governance, change management existing alongside or above the participant's own practice.
When to use: Use where an institutional process is named as distinct from the participant's personal workflow.
When not to use: Use Draft-then-ratify workflow instead for the personal or team-level drafting-to-publication process.

Definition: A proposed or practised discipline of re-reading the decision log to check whether its context still holds, whether anything has changed, or whether an update or supersession is now warranted.
When to use: Use for review-as-practice, whether already done or offered as a future direction.
When not to use: Use Staleness and non-revisiting instead for the bare observation of decay with no remedy attached.

Definition: Maintenance of the record stops when ownership moves to another team; the originators no longer track subsequent decisions and so stop updating, even though the record remains useful to the new owners.
When to use: Use where a transfer of ownership is given as the reason maintenance stops.
When not to use: Use Staleness and non-revisiting instead for decay with no ownership change involved.

Definition: ADRs are kept as plain text with no dedicated tooling, because the content should be simple enough that lightweight text is sufficient.
When to use: Use where the participant states or implies that plain text is the medium of choice, whether framed as an original intent, a version-control preference, or a felt sufficiency.
When not to use: Use Storage discoverability and canonical location instead for where that text lives and how it is found, as distinct from its being text in the first place.

Definition: ADR usefulness depends on where records live, whether they can be found, and whether a single canonical version is clear once drafts and published copies both exist.
When to use: Use for repository placement, the difficulty of choosing a location across many repositories (e.g. under microservices), canonical-version marking, and cross-linking practice such as preferring links to the canonical version over links to a superseded draft.
When not to use: Use Wiki and document tooling instead for which specific named tools are used, considered apart from findability. Use Boundary with supporting documents instead for what content belongs inline versus linked, which is an editorial rather than a storage question.

Definition: The specific named document and wiki tools actually used (Confluence, Google Docs, shared drives, slide decks, architecture documents) and how their features (commenting, page-per-ADR) are used.
When to use: Use for named tools and their features.
When not to use: Use Storage discoverability and canonical location instead for the findability/canonicality problem those tools are being used to solve, and Draft-then-ratify workflow for the stages the tools support.

Definition: Capability a participant would want from tooling that does not exist or is not in use (tracking which ADR elements are still incomplete or open, surfacing relationships between design issues, holistic cross-issue analysis), whether or not an LLM is the proposed mechanism.
When to use: Use for wished-for features not currently available, including per-element completeness tracking within a still-open ADR.
When not to use: Use Wiki and document tooling instead for tools already in use. Use LLM as consumer of the ADR corpus instead when the turn's substance is about what an LLM reading an existing corpus could do, rather than a wished-for tracking capability.

Definition: A concrete, reported instance of a later reader actually being helped by an existing ADR: onboarding, a reorganisation, a downstream team asking fewer questions, a successor learning from it. Distinct from the abstract statement of purpose (Rationale for future readers).
When to use: Use for reports of the benefit actually occurring, not merely being intended.
When not to use: Use Rationale for future readers instead for the abstract, stated purpose. Use Consultation occasions instead for the bare behavioural fact of when ADRs get opened, without a claim that it helped: the two frequently co-occur and may be double-coded.

Definition: The value of ADRs shows up over years, specifically when the people who made the original decisions are no longer there and new architects must reconstruct understanding without them.
When to use: Use for statements tying ADR importance to the long run, staff turnover, or legacy-system maintenance.
When not to use: Use Future-reader benefit observed instead for a concrete reported instance rather than a general claim about long-term value.

Definition: The participant explicitly declines to claim an effect on code quality, defect rates, or maintainability, citing absent evidence rather than offering an unsupported opinion.
When to use: Use for explicit non-answers of this kind.
When not to use: Use for answers that assert an effect only if the assertion itself is being coded elsewhere; this code is specifically for the refusal to assert.

Code: LLM as consumer of the ADR corpus
Definition: A language model used to read, summarise, interrogate, or relate an existing body of ADRs, rather than to author one or to review a specific draft before publication.
When to use: Use where the model's role is analysis or synthesis across records that already exist: summarising, answering speculative questions against the corpus, surfacing relationships between issues.
When not to use: Use LLM as quality checker instead when the model is reviewing one specific draft before it is published, rather than reading a corpus.

Definition: A model used to critique a human-written draft before publication (does the context support the decision, would a low-context reader follow it) functioning as a reviewer or rubber duck, not an author.
When to use: Use for review, rubber-ducking, or draft-checking roles specifically.
When not to use: Use LLM as consumer of the ADR corpus instead for post-publication reading/analysis across many records.

Code: Generated rationale is not the real rationale
Definition: A model asked to justify a decision produces plausible reasoning that is not the reasoning that actually operated: invented context, a different rationale on each asking, or a retroactive construction justifying something that was generated rather than decided. The danger is specifically that it reads as true.
When to use: Use for fabrication, non-determinism of generated rationale, inability to recover what a group actually thought, and consequent distrust of generated records or their rationale.
When not to use: Use Agent-generated architecture documentation instead when the complaint is about the whole document's quality (repetitive, incomplete, badly proportioned) rather than the rationale's authenticity specifically.

Definition: The architecture documentation coding agents write unprompted, assessed as an artefact (repetitive, self-contradictory, incomplete, badly proportioned), and what, if anything, makes it more tolerable (e.g. constraining it to mirror current code rather than reconstruct reasoning).
When to use: Use for assessments of generated documentation's quality as a whole document, including mitigations and proposals to study it empirically.
When not to use: Use Generated rationale is not the real rationale instead for the narrower claim that the reasoning specifically is fabricated.

Code: Practice shaped by mentors or literature
Definition: The participant's own way of writing ADRs traces to a mentor, senior colleague, book, blog post, or institutional literature, rather than to formal ADR-specific training.
When to use: Use for training, reading, and crediting an individual, book, or institution as the source of the participant's practice, including authorship of a named format.
When not to use: Use Governance and template ownership instead for present-tense institutional ownership of templates, as distinct from the historical origin of the participant's own habits.

Definition: The observation that ADRs are rare in practice at all, offered as context that lowers the bar against which any given ADR is judged.
When to use: Use where scarcity of the practice itself is offered as part of a quality judgement.
When not to use: Use Handover maintenance gap instead for a specific team's ADRs going unmaintained, which is a different claim from the general rarity of the practice.

Code: Significance threshold for writing an ADR
Definition: A practice, or a normative claim, that ADRs should be written only for decisions that are significant or non-obvious, not for every minor choice. The anti-pattern is over-application to trivial decisions; the positive practice is deliberate selectivity.
When to use: Use where the participant states or implies a threshold of significance or non-obviousness a decision must cross before it warrants a record, whether describing the positive practice of reserving ADRs for such decisions or naming the anti-pattern of writing too many for minor ones.
When not to use: Use for general remarks about decision-making that do not bear on whether a decision crosses the bar for having a record made of it. Use Effort scaled to decision impact and project context instead for the separate question of how much rigor a decision that has already cleared the bar should get.

Code: Effort scaled to decision impact and project context
Definition: How much documentation effort and dissemination a decision gets, and how formal the overall ADR practice needs to be, should scale with the decision's impact and with the project's size, duration, and team, rather than being applied uniformly.
When to use: Use where the participant ties documentation effort, formality, or dissemination breadth to either the significance of a specific decision or to overall project or team scale and context, including the existence threshold (whether anything needs to be written down at all below some team size).
When not to use: Use Significance threshold for writing an ADR instead for the separate yes/no question of whether a decision warrants a record at all, independent of project scale.

Definition: Some teams treat an accepted ADR as open to occasional addition, coming back to add explanatory commentary to its body, rather than strictly frozen. Distinct from Immutability and superseding, which covers the status and supersession mechanism, not commentary added to an existing record.
When to use: Use where a participant describes adding to or annotating an ADR after acceptance, short of a formal supersession.
When not to use: Use Immutability and superseding instead for the stricter regime where content is never touched after acceptance and change happens only via a new, linked record.

Code: Skepticism toward LLM automation of ADR writing
Definition: A participant argues that using an LLM to automate or accelerate the writing of ADRs is not worthwhile, because the cost of building, maintaining, training people on, and validating the output of such automation exceeds the cost of simply writing ADRs manually.
When to use: Use for explicit cost/benefit skepticism about LLM-driven ADR authoring specifically, not reading or analysis.
When not to use: Use LLM as quality checker or LLM as consumer of the ADR corpus instead for endorsed uses of LLMs with ADRs.

Code: Political pressure distorts the recorded rationale
Definition: The reason actually recorded in an ADR is not the true reason for the decision, because organisational politics, internal conflict, or the inability to state an uncomfortable truth lead the author to write a more acceptable, sanitised rationale instead.
When to use: Use where the participant describes a gap between the stated and the real reason for a decision, attributed to internal conflict, politics, or an inability to be candid.
When not to use: Use Speculative or political content instead when the complaint is about political material being present in the ADR, not about a missing or false rationale. Use Generated rationale is not the real rationale instead when the false rationale comes from a model rather than organisational pressure.

Definition: In large, process-heavy organisations, documentation gets written not because it is valued but because a rule or process requires it, done to satisfy the requirement rather than to actually communicate anything.
When to use: Use where the participant describes documentation produced to comply with an imposed process or organisational rigidity rather than out of genuine motivation, especially when attributed to large or rigid organisations.
When not to use: Use Governance and template ownership instead for institutional ownership described neutrally, without the box-checking or resentment framing.

Definition: A good ADR records who made the decision and when, and carries a short, well-chosen, descriptive name or title, as basic identifying metadata distinct from the substantive content.
When to use: Use where the participant lists date-made, author/owner, or a unique title/name as a required element of the record.
When not to use: Use Status and lifecycle marking instead for the approval/superseded state field specifically, not identifying metadata. Use Structure as scaffolding instead for content-bearing sections (issue, alternatives, decision, consequences) rather than identifying metadata.

Definition: What counts as an architecturally significant decision spans a range of granularity, from major structural choices down to coding conventions, design patterns, and component- or class-level choices.
When to use: Use where the participant explicitly discusses decisions or their documentation spanning multiple levels (architecture-wide vs. component vs. class/pattern level), or blurs the line between 'architectural' and lower-level decisions.
When not to use: Use Significance threshold for writing an ADR instead for the separate question of whether a decision, at any level, is significant/non-obvious enough to warrant a record.

Definition: A decision record need not be a formal written document: a photo of a whiteboard sketch, a diagram, or notes from an in-person meeting count as legitimate documentation of a decision, provided the team can refer back to them.
When to use: Use where the participant explicitly extends 'documentation' to non-textual or informal artifacts (photos, sketches, meeting notes) as sufficient.
When not to use: Use Wiki and document tooling instead for named formal documentation platforms, even lightweight ones.

Definition: Excessive focus on structure, templates, and formatting displaces the substantive content that actually matters, including the specific case of trade-off documentation being reduced to filling in a table's structure rather than capturing the trade-off.
When to use: Use where the participant names structure, format, or template compliance as crowding out real content.
When not to use: Use Structure as scaffolding instead for the positive endorsement of structure, and Decision section as design document for the opposite content problem (too much design detail rather than too little substance).

Definition: The record itself is poorly crafted regardless of staleness: unproofread, internally inconsistent, careless. A defect of authoring quality distinct from the record simply going out of date.
When to use: Use where the participant names lack of proofreading, inconsistency, or carelessness in the writing itself as the problem.
When not to use: Use Staleness and non-revisiting instead for decay or outdatedness over time rather than a quality defect present from the start.

Definition: Decisions get written up as the first idea that came to mind, without being debated or checked by a second or third opinion: the anti-pattern mirror of Writing forces deliberation.
When to use: Use where the participant names a lack of debate or review before a decision was written down as the problem.
When not to use: Use Writing forces deliberation instead for the positive claim that the act of writing itself induces deliberation.

Code: Informal chat as de facto decision record
Definition: In practice, architectural decisions get communicated, and effectively 'recorded', through ephemeral channels such as chat messages or messaging-app threads rather than a dedicated document, and this is treated as a real, if suboptimal, form of the practice rather than an absence of one.
When to use: Use where the participant describes chat or messaging as the actual mechanism decisions get communicated or recorded through, especially where no dedicated document exists.
When not to use: Use Wiki and document tooling instead for named, persistent documentation tools, even lightweight ones.

Definition: Sustaining the practice of writing ADRs is described as requiring ongoing individual or team discipline; without it, decisions get made and enacted without ever being written down, regardless of tooling or the existence of a template.
When to use: Use where the participant attributes non-adoption or inconsistent practice to a lack of discipline or habit, rather than to tooling, process, or knowledge gaps.
When not to use: Use Handover maintenance gap instead for a specific ownership-transfer cause of non-maintenance, or Low baseline of ADR adoption for the general rarity claim without the discipline framing.

Definition: Establishing a documentation culture, including ADRs, requires a champion who makes the case for it and management support that treats documentation as worth paying for in time and cost.
When to use: Use where the participant frames adoption as contingent on leadership advocacy and/or management willingness to fund documentation work.
When not to use: Use Governance and template ownership instead for existing institutional process or ownership, described neutrally, rather than the case for winning support and funding it.

Code: Undocumented decisions cause duplicated or conflicting solutions
Definition: Without a visible record, large or long-running systems end up with multiple, inconsistent solutions to the same problem, different teams solving it differently because nobody could see what was already decided and why.
When to use: Use where the participant reports or predicts this specific concrete consequence of missing ADRs.
When not to use: Use Long-term maintainability and turnover instead for the general value-over-years claim without this specific duplication or conflict mechanism.

Definition: An LLM's usefulness for a specific system or domain depends on how much relevant material exists in its training data; for niche, under-documented, or highly specific systems, the model has little to draw on and is expected to add less value.
When to use: Use where the participant reasons about whether an LLM would help based on public or training-data availability for a specific domain.
When not to use: Use Generated rationale is not the real rationale instead for fabrication or inconsistency concerns, rather than coverage-gap reasoning.

Definition: Software always has an architecture, whether explicit or implicit; the value of writing decisions down is specifically in converting tacit, implicit architectural choices into an explicit, examinable form: a team can only benefit from an architecture once it is made explicit.
When to use: Use where the participant frames the core value of ADRs around explicitness itself (turning tacit/implicit decisions visible) rather than around future readers or the deliberative act of writing.
When not to use: Use Writing forces deliberation instead for the claim that writing improves the decision-making process itself, or Rationale for future readers for the future-reader-benefit framing. Use Context and rationale for the decision instead once the record's necessity is assumed and the question is what it should contain.

Definition: An LLM is used to generate the initial structure or scaffolding of a new ADR from a given template and some context, so the author doesn't start from a blank page; the human still supplies and edits the substantive content.
When to use: Use where the participant describes using an LLM to produce a first-draft skeleton/scaffolding for a new ADR from a template, which a human then fills in or edits.
When not to use: Use LLM as quality checker instead for reviewing an already-written draft, Agent-generated architecture documentation instead for fuller, unprompted generation of documentation from code, and LLM-drafted ADRs default to verbose for the specific complaint that generated drafts are bloated.

Code: Risk of losing future expert judgment to AI substitution
Definition: If AI increasingly substitutes for architects' work, there is a risk that fewer people accumulate the experience needed to become expert architects in the future: a long-run capability-pipeline concern, distinct from concerns about the quality of AI-generated content itself.
When to use: Use where the participant raises the risk that AI displacing architectural work reduces the number of people who develop architectural expertise over time.
When not to use: Use LLM domain-coverage limits or Generated rationale is not the real rationale instead for concerns about the AI's output quality rather than the human expertise pipeline. Use Technical-writing competence instead for a narrower claim about writing skill specifically.

Definition: ADRs are written primarily to give a coding agent shared, persistent context during active development (so the agent doesn't need to re-derive decisions each session and produces fewer wasted iterations) rather than, or in addition to, being written for human readers. The ADR functions as externalised memory for the agent's working context, and even section ordering is described as affecting the agent's reasoning-token efficiency when consuming it.
When to use: Use where the participant frames the ADR's purpose or value around supplying context to an AI coding assistant/agent during implementation, distinct from an LLM reading, reviewing, or generating documentation after the fact.
When not to use: Use Rationale for future readers or Future-reader benefit observed instead when the audience is explicitly human. Use LLM as consumer of the ADR corpus instead for post-hoc reading/analysis of an existing corpus, and Agent-generated architecture documentation instead for the agent producing documentation from code.

Definition: A reader's trust in an ADR is tied to visible evidence that it was reviewed and approved by recognised subject-matter experts or a formal decision board: seeing who signed off, not just what was decided, is what establishes the record's credibility.
When to use: Use where the participant ties the trustworthiness or reusability of an ADR to an approval workflow, named reviewers, or a governance board's sign-off.
When not to use: Use Decision metadata: authorship, date, title instead for the simple fact of recording who made the decision, without the trust/credibility framing. Use Governance and template ownership instead for institutional process described without this authenticity angle.

Code: Structured trade-off fields: pros, cons, assumptions
Definition: A template that documents trade-offs through discrete, separate fields (advantages, disadvantages, assumptions or premises, and the specific quality attributes traded off against each other) rather than open prose. Presented as good, standard practice. It is kept apart from Consequences reduced to pros and cons on purpose: participants disagree here (some reject the pro/con framing, others endorse structured pros, cons and assumptions), and the two codes preserve that disagreement.
When to use: Use where the participant describes or endorses breaking trade-off documentation into discrete structured fields (pros/cons/assumptions/quality-attribute trade-off) as a template design choice, including reported difficulty applying the distinction (e.g. novices confusing 'disadvantage' with 'trade-off').
When not to use: Use Consequences reduced to pros and cons instead when the participant is specifically criticising evaluative pro/con framing as a defect.

Definition: When asked to write an ADR, an LLM tends to produce an overly verbose, unfocused draft, because the reasoning behind a design decision is not something that derives easily or is typically written down anywhere the model can read it; without the author manually feeding a great deal of condensed context, the output has to be trimmed back down by hand to be usable.
When to use: Use where the participant describes LLM-generated ADR drafts as too long or unfocused specifically, requiring manual editing down, as a structural mismatch with the format's own goal of being focused and concise.
When not to use: Use Skepticism toward LLM automation of ADR writing instead for a cost/benefit argument against automating ADR writing at all, and LLM as drafting scaffolder for a positive account of using an LLM for structural scaffolding.

Definition: An AI coding agent, working from its own persistent understanding of a codebase and its history of decisions, proactively identifies which existing ADRs are affected by a change it's implementing, and updates or supersedes them (cross-linking the new record) with limited manual effort from the developer: a realised, not merely wished-for, version of self-maintaining documentation.
When to use: Use where the participant describes this as something actually happening in their current workflow, not a hoped-for future capability.
When not to use: Use Desired tool capability instead for the same idea when it's unrealised or wished-for rather than actually practised.

Definition: An ADR states a quality goal ('good performance', 'this improves scalability') without concrete, testable criteria for what counts as meeting it, so a reader cannot tell whether the goal was actually achieved or even what achieving it would look like.
When to use: Use where the participant criticises an ADR (or a class of ADRs) for stating a quality attribute or goal without a concrete, checkable criterion.
When not to use: Use Missing rationale instead for reasoning that is absent altogether, rather than present but unfalsifiable. Use Grounding in critical use cases and quality attributes instead for the positive practice of tying decisions to specific, named quality attributes.

Code: ADRs should be scoped to one decision
Definition: A good ADR addresses exactly one decision; combining several distinct decisions into a single record makes it unclear what was actually decided and accepted, and is named independently by two participants as a specific, avoidable failure mode.
When to use: Use where the participant states or implies that an ADR should cover a single decision, or criticises a record for cramming multiple decisions together.
When not to use: Use Decisions at multiple granularities instead for the separate, non-evaluative observation that decisions exist at different architectural levels (system vs. component vs. class) and can be organised hierarchically (e.g. a parent ADR with sub-ADRs): that pattern is compatible with, not a violation of, one-decision-per-record scoping.

Definition: A good ADR states not only what a decision or pattern is for and when to apply it, but also when NOT to apply it: an explicit boundary of applicability, treated as an anti-pattern statement equally important as the positive pattern, and as something participants find difficult to write.
When to use: Use where the participant describes stating a decision's or pattern's non-applicability, boundary conditions, or 'when not to use this' as a required or valuable ADR element.
When not to use: Use Rejected alternatives and why instead for options that were considered and not chosen: this code is about the boundary of the option that WAS chosen, not about alternatives to it.

Code: AI homogenises architecture toward vendor-favouring defaults
Definition: Coding agents and copilots, trained on whatever architectural patterns and terminology are prevalent in their training data, systematically default to one way of doing architecture (often favouring approaches that lock an organisation into a hyperscaler's ecosystem) and do not surface alternatives unless explicitly prompted to. Distinct from fabrication (Generated rationale is not the real rationale) and from coverage gaps in niche domains (LLM domain-coverage limits): this is about systematic bias toward the mainstream/vendor-favoured option even in well-covered domains.
When to use: Use where the participant describes an AI tool defaulting to a single architectural approach, failing to surface alternatives, reinterpreting or 'hijacking' the team's own terminology toward its training data's conventions, or steering toward vendor lock-in.
When not to use: Use Generated rationale is not the real rationale instead for fabricated or invented justification, and LLM domain-coverage limits instead for an honest coverage gap in an under-represented domain rather than a bias toward an over-represented one.

Definition: A participant, while open to LLM support, holds that the ADR should still be written by a thoughtful human being, because that authorship is the key element of a good record.
When to use: Use where the participant says a person, not a model, should write the ADR, or that human thought is what makes the record work, even when LLMs are not excluded for other roles.
When not to use: Use Generated rationale is not the real rationale instead when the point is that a model's rationale is fabricated or untrustworthy; use Writing forces deliberation instead when the point is that writing improves the author's own thinking, with no contrast to LLMs.

Code: Time pressure and overhead as barrier
Definition: Documentation, including ADRs, gets skipped, abandoned or left un-updated because of daily workload, deadlines or the perceived overhead of writing it, rather than for lack of tooling, knowledge or discipline.
When to use: Use where the participant attributes lapses in writing or updating documentation to lack of time, deadlines or overhead.
When not to use: Use Discipline as adoption barrier instead when the cause is framed as lack of habit or discipline, and Management sponsorship and budget when the issue is funding or leadership support.
